messages.author: 8753e7ce2213ca31
messages.subject: repeated transects in dsm
parts:
Hi all,

I want to use DSM to develop a map of abundance of livestock in my study area. I have aerial data of livestock (8 transects lines) surveyed four times in a year (december, february, june and august) (I acknowledge that 8 transect could be a small sample size, but the study area is small and they cover it well, so I hope it may be not too bad.). In each survey, I repeated the same 8 transects. So, I have 8 x 4 surveyed transects. I am interested in annual density, not in density by time periods. I was reading that one alternative is to pool all data from the 4 repeated visits into a single line transect prior to analysis, and to record the effort as transect length multiplied by 4 visits (as is explained in the book Introduction of Distance Sampling, pag 79). My concern with this alternative is twofold:

(1) the repeated visits are not close in time, they are in different months in a year and could be a change in density between periods.

(2) regarding using DSM, if I pool the data from 4 visits, I will have animal counts of different time periods in the same segment that will be correlated in time. Since dsm have a spatial component, and the position where the animal was observed is key, I am not sure whether multiplying the segment effort by 4 times will be correct and real. What do you think? How can I work with that?

Any help with this will be very appreciated.

Natalia M. Schroeder

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] repeated transects in dsm
parts:
Natalia

You raise some useful issues.  However two of your statements seem inconsistent with each other "I am interested in annual density, not in density by time periods" and "could be a change in density between periods".  If statement 2 is true, then statement 1 is in doubt.

Commonly, repeat visits are used to produce sufficient detections to reliably estimate the detection function.  Pooling data across visits produces an estimate of average density/abundance across visits.

If you do pool the visits, then you should multiply effort by the number of visits.  In the case of density surface modelling, the effort that is relevant is the size of the segments into which the transects have been cut.  The response variable being modelled by the density surface is something akin to number of animals inside a segment after adjusting for imperfect detectability.  If the repeated visits is not incorporated into the transect length (and hence into the segment lengths), this response variable will not be correct.

You raise a good point about temporal correlation.  Spatio-temporal models (see email to this list from Dave Miller on 29 March 2016) could address this, but as Dave says, this is still is the 'experimental' stage.

I hope that is of some use to you.
